speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MEETINGS OF COMMITTEE OF PARLIAMENTARIANS, SCIENTISTS AND ENGINEERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Committee of Parliamentarians, Scientists and Engineers, under the acronym COPSE, was set up in order to facilitate the interaction of parliamentarians with the scientific and engineering community. It has organized noon-hour information lunches on the second Tuesday of each month on issues of interest to scientists and parliamentarians. This mixed audience is spared as much as possible the "difficult to understand" technical jargon. Outstanding workers in the scientific field are invited speakers.
There are only a handful of parliamentarians who have a background in science, yet we live in an unprecedented age of information and technical change which, in a span of one generation, will have a revolutionary effect on Canadian society. Members of Parliament have an opportunity to make themselves aware of advances in science, medicine and technology which are changing the lifestyles, work habits and economic relationships of all Canadians. It is the task of Parliament to prepare the climate for such a change.
Until such time as a parliamentary standing committee on science and technology comes about, the monthly meetings of COPSE provide extremely worth-while forums for Members of Parliament to become knowledgeable on issues affecting the lives of all their constituents. I am concerned that so few Members of Parliament are supporting the COPSE initiative to help this nation assert itself in the age of technology and information.

Unlike any other office in the country, the Prime Minister's Office has unlimited power to secure information.
We now learn about an official in the Prime Minister's Office being instructed to go to different government Departments to ask for and obtain confidential information, personal

and private, about the Leader of the Opposition. No Member of Parliament can or should have access to the confidential files of Departments of Government; no research office of other Parties can make that demand. What they have access to is in the public domain. What the Prime Minister's Office has access to is in the confidential domain. That is the difference.
We have seen the nature of that confidential material being raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) as a threat against the Leader of the Opposition. subsubtopic: PROVISION OF WATER SUPPLY FOR DAUPHIN, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, attempts by the Town of Dauphin to obtain a long-term lease for the use of Lake Edwards in Riding Mountain National Park as a backup water supply source so far have proved fruitless. Negotiations between the Town of Dauphin and Parks Canada officials have been deadlocked since 1979.
Historically the Town of Dauphin has used Lake Edwards in Riding Mountain National Park as a water supply source long before a national park was established in the Riding Mountains.
Parks Canada wants to force the town to abandon the lake if it cannot document its current and projected need for the water from the lake, to its satisfaction. The problem has reached the stage where park officials have been restricting town maintenance crews' access to the dykes for repair work. This is a pressing problem which has dragged on far too long. I call upon the Minister to act personally to resolve this problem and guarantee Dauphin's future water supply.

subsubtopic: BUDGET BUSINESS TAX PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance certain questions about the unfairness of the Budget as it affects pensioners and middle and low income Canadians. He replied with disarming candour, saying that is how the tax system works. Well, the Liberal tax system, I guess.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister questions about unfairness again today as it affects a certain bonanza that is being given to large corporations. As a result of the new Budget, Eaton's and Bata, which are hardly corner stores, are now going to qualify as small businesses. They will be able to be taxed at the small business tax rate of 15 per cent. As a result of tax increases imposed by the Minister of Finance's last Budget, average families will have to pay about $500 more per family. Is it the Government's idea of fairness that the $500 increase for the ordinary Canadian should make up for the thousands of dollars which are going to be lost to the tax system from companies like Bata and Eaton's?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: BUDGET BUSINESS TAX PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member is misconstruing the provision in the Budget regarding small business. The proposition is quite simple. It is to simplify the whole tax structure and not have artificial categories about small and larger businesses. The principle of taxing larger businesses at a different rate is maintained in the Budget. Eaton's obviously does not qualify as a small business. The first couple of hundred thousand dollars of its business are perhaps considered as small for simplification of tax purposes. However, everything above that is taxed at a different rate. The Hon. Member is miscontruing the meaning of the Budget. He would do well to reread the section.

income to richer Canadians instead of moving toward justice for middle and low income Canadians?

subsubtopic: PENSION ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR WIDOWS OF OFFICERS KILLED ON DUTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member has forgotten it, but in the last four years I have been Solicitor General I have introduced a substantial improvement in the pensions available for widows and children of RCMP officers slain while on duty, if the risk which resulted in their death was one of those special risks which they face when they go to work every day that other public servants and other members of the public do not face. I have told the Hon. When those risks result in their death, society should recognize that. That is the basis of the policy, and that is the reason why widows and orphans whose fathers and husbands die in those special circumstances receive enhanced pension benefits.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA INDIAN CUT-OFF LANDS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to address the House on second reading of Bill C-18, an Act to provide for the settlement of claims by Indian bands in British Columbia relating to certain lands cut off from their reserves.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill concerns the settlement of a particular kind of land claims made by Indian bands in British Columbia. They are referred to as the cut-off lands claims.
Members from British Columbia will recall that twenty-two Indian bands in that province have for a long time been seeking to obtain the right to compensation for lands cut off from their reserves, without their consent, in 1920.
The primary objective of this Bill is to give the Indian bands concerned the power to enter into agreements with the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia in order to settle these claims. Mr. Speaker, this legislation will confirm existing agreements and give them force of law. It will also authorize the Governor in Council to enter into future agreements.
Mr. Speaker, I feel this Bill deserves to be approved by all Members of this House, and I wish to give my reasons for asking the House to support this legislation.
First of all, there are pressing reasons for bringing this Bill to your attention at this time. In fact, when an agreement was

February 17, 1984
Lands Settlement Act
signed nearly two years ago by the federal Government, the Government of British Columbia and the Penticton Band, it was understood that the necessary federal legislation would have to be passed by March 6, 1984. If that condition is not met, the Government of British Columbia will no longer be bound to give the band its share of financial compensation and transfer of land to the band will be delayed. However, the Government of British Columbia, pending adoption of federal legislation, has agreed to give back to the band nearly 5,000 hectares of reserve land and to pay the band $1.2 million. Mr. Speaker, that is why this Bill is now a priority. The Bill should have been submitted earlier for second reading, but when the draft legislation was tabled in the House last June, a number of bands asked for changes. Since everyone agreed on the nature of the amendments, the Bill was redrafted. The cut-off lands episode explains why the Indians doubted the good faith of the two governments concerned and the rationale of their policies and methods. Before and after British Columbia entered Confederation in 1871, some Crown land had been set aside for the Indian bands. From the outset, the federal Government and the government of the new province had differences of opinion regarding the size of the reserves. The province maintained that federal plans for establishing large reserves would adversely affect the establishment of new settlers and their activities. According to the province, the area taken up by mountains and forests would greatly reduce the amount of land suitable for settlement. To resolve this question, in 1912 the federal Government appointed Mr. J. A. McKenna as Special Commissioner, who was to meet a number of times with Sir Richard McBride, the Premier of British Columbia, and the result of these meetings was what became known as the McKenna-McBride Agreement.
Mr. Speaker, this Agreement provided for the creation of a Royal Commission of Inquiry. The Commission consisted of five members, and its mandate was to settle the reserve question by means of significant changes:
1.	To cut off from the reserves any land that did not really meet a specific need, with the consent of the Indians;
2.	To add lands to reserves that were too small;
3.	To create new Indian reserves as appropriate.
According to the Agreement, Mr. Speaker, the cut-off lands would be sold and the proceeds shared equally between both governments. The federal Government's share was to be used for the benefit of the bands concerned. The Commission held hearings throughout British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be allowed to read part of a speech made in June 1913 by the Chairman of the Commission to Indians on the Capilano Reserve:
If a reserve includes a portion of land that is in excess of the actual needs of the Indians living on the reserve, the Commission will determine the portion of land to be cut off. However, said portion may be withdrawn only with the consent of the Indians concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is clear there was an obligation to consult members of the bands concerned before cutting off a single portion of land from the reserves. Because of these guarantees, which were repeated and put in writing many times, the band chiefs were co-operative and well disposed in their discussions with the Commission.
At a meeting of the Metlakatla Band in 1915, the Chief stated as follows:
We want the Indian reserve of Metlakatla to enjoy a measure of security. We do not agree with the young people who want lands to be cut off from our reserve. However, we do not, for the time being, wish to speak out publicly against this plan. We leave it to you to decide what is best for us, and we want to protect our reserve.
Mr. Speaker, the McKenna-McBride Commission submitted its report three years later, in 1916. However, immediately after the report was published, the British Columbia Legislative Assembly adopted the Indian Affairs Settlement Act, and in 1920, the Parliament of Canada passed the British Columbia Indian Lands Settlement Act. This Act, however, eliminated the need to obtain the consent of the bands.
That is what has caused discontent among the Indians of British Columbia for over 60 years. Mr. Speaker, the twenty-two bands concerned consider this a violation of the McKenna-McBride Agreement, since the lands were, in fact, cut off without their consent.
Since that time, their chiefs have never ceased to urge both governments to settle their claims and give back the lands. Finally, in 1969, although technically not responsible, the federal Government agreed to negotiate a settlement. Federal and provincial authorities started discussions, and in 1977, the two governments started tripartite negotiations with a committee representing the twenty-two bands.
At the beginning of 1981, Mr. Speaker, the committee decided it was unable to pursue negotiations for the time being. At this point, the individual bands, on the basis of general principles previously agreed to, started to negotiate directly with both levels of government. Among other things, it was agreed that where feasible, the lands originally cut off would be returned to the bands. The land claims cover over
12,000	hectares, but about 10 per cent of the cut-off lands will not be given back to the Indians.
The federal Government will pay compensation for lands that are now the property of a third party. The Province is already offering compensation for cut-off lands it wishes to keep for public use, as well as compensation for damages caused over the years on cut-off lands that are to be returned to the Indians.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members will probably be interested to hear some details of the agreements concluded to date with six of the bands, to improve their understanding of this Bill.
February 17, 1984

First, more than 4,900 hectares of land will be returned to the Penticton Band, the first one to reach a settlement. The Band will also receive about $13 million from the Government of Canada and $1.2 million from British Columbia.
The Osoyoos Band will receive $634,000 from the Government of Canada and nearly $360,000 from the Government of British Columbia. In addition, about 70 hectares of land will be returned to the Clinton Band, which will also receive $10,000 from the Province of British Columbia and $140,000 from the Government of Canada.
The Westbank Band will recover 22 hectares of land plus $7 million paid by the Government of Canada and about $1 million from the Government of British Columbia.
The Squamish Band will receive over 45 hectares of land, almost $1 million from the Canadian Government and more than one-half million dollars from British Columbia.
Finally, the Okanagan Band will receive 27 hectares of land, plus $1.4 million from the Government of Canada and $32,000 from British Columbia. This settlement has yet to be ratified by the Band.
Mr. Speaker, behind these figures there is a depth of feeling that cannot be quantified. At a signing ceremony attended by the Band Chiefs of the Westbank, Okanagan and Squamish bands, and the Attorney General of British Columbia, this is what Chief Mathias of the Squamish Band said, and I quote:
Now our people can once more walk the 115 acres of the Capilano Squamish reserve and face the sun with pride. This is a historic event.
Chief Mathias went on:
The struggle is almost over, and it warms my heart to see the Attorney General of British Columbia and the Minister of Indian Affairs of Canada signing an agreement with us on the matter of the cut-off lands.
Mr. Speaker, at this point I would like to emphasize the important role played by British Columbia. Without the good will and co-operation of this Province, the problem would never have been resolved.
Mr. Speaker, the Province has provided millions of dollars, but also and more important, it has provided for the transfer of
12,000	hectares of land which can now be returned to the descendants of the original population, once this legislation is passed. Agreements signed up to now have shown once again that the Government of British Columbia and the Government of Canada can work together to serve the native peoples of this Province. The work done by British Columbia is invaluable, and there will be further meetings with the Attorney General of the Province to sign other land claims settlements.
Among all the parties concerned, the band chiefs have had the most important role to play. Through patience, perseverance and determination, they have now been able to recover their lands.
Lands Settlement Act
I would like to say a few words about the urgent aspect of this Bill and the negotiations that followed the tabling of the draft legislation last June. In the course of negotiations between Canada, British Columbia and the Penticton Band, we all agreed to include a provision stipulating that special federal and provincial legislation would become effective within two years after the agreement was approved by the Band by means of a referendum. Mr. Speaker, the Penticton Band approved the agreement by referendum on March 6, 1982, and the Legislative Assembly of the Province of British Columbia passed a Bill in July of that year concerning the cut-off Indian lands. The agreement concluded with the Penticton Band, and with many others, contains a provision that funds payable to the Band by the Province are to be held in trust for two years.
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that if the federal legislation is not enacted between now and March 6, 1984-within 15 days-the $1 million held in trust for the Penticton Band and the $200,000 in interests on that money will go to the province. As you recall, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that more than
12,000	hectares of land will be returned to the 22 bands. Those lands cannot be returned to the province before this Bill is passed, which goes to show how urgent the adoption of this measure has become, Mr. Speaker.
Proposed legislation dealing with those agreements was tabled in the House on June 14, 1983. That decision was taken because a number of bands had made it clear that they would not sign any agreement nor even continue the negotiations before seeing a copy of the draft legislation. When the proposed legislation was tabled, some bands began to wonder whether the Bill might not have something to do with all sorts of claims. Such was not the purpose of the Bill which had been drafted so as to allow only for the settlement of claims concerning cut-off lands. We negotiated with the band spokesmen to allay their fears. The bands were particularly worried about an expression contained in the proposed legislation. It had to do with the status of reserve lands between 1871 and 1938 and read as follows:
-that the Province of British Columbia had designated for the use and benefit of Indians-
After lengthy consultations, Mr. Speaker, the expression was changed and now reads as follows:
-set aside for the use and benefit of Indians-
But the Indians had other worries, Mr. Speaker. Among others, one of their concerns was that the law might be interpreted to apply to lands other than cut-off lands. To meet that objection, we added a seventh clause, as follows:
Nothing in this Act affects any claims asserted by a band or the council of the band other than claims in respect of cut-off lands.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to tell the Hon. Member that, following these amendments, we received last December a letter from the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs informing us that all the bands but one had withdrawn their objections to this draft. We are now negotiating with the band

February 17, 1984
Lands Settlement Act
still objecting to the draft and we hope to reach an agreement in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we now have a better proposal which has been accepted by all the parties involved, namely the Province of British Columbia, the Government of Canada, and more importantly, the bands and native associations.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation must be passed without delay because, as I have already mentioned, these agreements include a provision for prescription after two years. In the case of the Penticton Band, this two-year period will end this coming March 6. If the legislation is not passed at that time, the band will loose $1 million plus $200,000 in interests and will not recover its lands. The same applies to the other agreements which have been signed. We are getting close to the end of the prescription period, Mr. Speaker, and these bands are running the risk of losing similar amounts.
Their impatience is therefore quite understandable and legitimate.
As I was saying, a few days ago, we received a letter from the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs urging us to pass the legislation before the second anniversary of the Penticton agreement. The Chiefs believe that if this legislation is not passed, it will cause prejudice to the bands and the spirit of the negotiations will not be respected. I must add that this Bill, which allows us to make good some of the inequities which still affect 10,000 registered Indians who are also our fellow-citizens, deserves to be supported by everyone. In this way, those who live on these lands will be able to continue to work on building a better future.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to close by quoting comments made recently by Chief Murray Alexis at a signing ceremony. He said the following:
What I can already foresee is that relations will improve between our communities. Whatever our racial origins, whether we are of the first founding nations or of the newcomers, we may be able today to begin everything afresh and build this country together.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for the welfare of the Indians of British Columbia, I ask that Bill C-18 be passed quickly so that finally justice may come to the native peoples of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to start again. This is the first opportunity I have had to address the House as official spokesman for Her Majesty's loyal opposition on matters concerning the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It is a pleasure for me to take part in the debate on Bill C-18, an Act to provide for the settlement of claims by Indian bands in British Columbia relating to certain lands cut off from their reserves.
Our Party supports this Bill, Mr. Speaker. We understand the urgency and we will not delay it unduly. As a matter of fact, our Party will assure that it receives all three readings and passage some time today. However, I am extremely disappointed that the Bill has been brought in so late and that the Parliamentary Secretary made it sound as though the Opposition was holding up the Bill. Nothing is further from the truth. The Government controls the timetable of the House. This Bill was just recently introduced to the House, and it is somewhat typical of the actions of this Government to bring Bills in at the last moment thus causing great unsettlement among the Indian bands who are going to derive some monetary benefits from these settlements. It could have been introduced and passed much earlier.
I might add that the Minister sees fit not to be here today, Mr. Speaker. He wrote me a letter explaining that he had other commitments. My concern is that the commitment is to the Liberal Party of the Northwest Territories, not to the 22 Indian bands of British Columbia affected by this very important legislation. I am very disappointed that he is fulfilling a political commitment to the Liberal Association of the Northwest Territories rather than fulfilling his parliamentary responsibility to be here to discuss this very important Bill.
I might say also that the briefing notes I received from the Department were all in Imperial measure, describing the lands as acreage. I noticed the Parliamentary Secretary went to metric. It will be very interesting to find out what standard they are using over there in the Ministry. This Government is so hep on the metric system, and the Parliamentary Secretary used it today, yet all the briefing notes refer to acreage. Therefore the House will pardon me if I discuss acreage today.
I think most of us understand that a little better in any event.
We are talking today about cut-off lands. We are not talking about original land claims, the comprehensive or specific claims presently being discussed throughout the country. We are talking about lands taken either by government survey, federal Orders in Council or just encroachment on Indian reserve lands which have been set up since around the 1860s. These lands were taken without consultation and without the permission of the Indian bands affected. There are 22 bands involved and, as the Parliamentary Secretary explained, 16 are being negotiated at the present time, five have been settled and one is under review. Although I should not speak for my friends to the left, both geographically and philosophically, I think it is fair to say that all three Parties want to correct the injustice committed here and restore to the native people in
February 17, 1984

British Columbia that which is rightfully theirs. There is no question that the land belongs to the bands and that compensation must be made.
On January 29, Mr. Speaker, I had a very enjoyable visit to the Penticton band reserve. I had the pleasure of accompanying the Member of Parliament for that area, the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), to Penticton.
I met with Chief Steward Phillip, Louise Eneas and Emory Gabriel. Because of my specific involvement with that particular band and the importance of this Bill to them, I would just like to relate my experience there in late January. They have coming to them from the British Columbia Government some $1 million, together with some $200,000 in interest which has built up over the past two years while the money was held in trust. They have also received in federal compensation some $13 million. They will realize a little over $14.6 million in compensation, together with 12,211 acres. Part of the 14,207 acres cut off is now the Penticton airport as well as a housing development.
This band, Mr. Speaker, has a beautiful reserve high in the hills overlooking Penticton in the Okanagan Valley. Under the leadership of Chief Stewart Phillip, they have wisely invested the moneys received to date. They just erected on their reserve 40 brand-new homes which members of the band will be paying for but which, of course, will be built with the help of the interest from the invested moneys. These homes are magnificent, some 1,000 or 1,100 square feet in area. The band is investing and spending the money in a responsible way and I gather they are very pleased with what has transpired. They were, naturally, very concerned that this Bill would not get through the House in time for them to receive the money the British Columbia Government holds for them. Of course, as 1 stated earlier today, we will allay those fears as we pass this legislation through the House in all three stages.
There are a number of matters which have not been solved as yet and negotiations are ongoing. I urge the federal Government to accelerate the tripartite negotiations which are going on. I realize that the British Columbia Government is involved as well. I have taken the liberty of speaking to the attorney general from British Columbia on this subject. He is anxious to carry out the negotiations, to ensure that this Bill is passed and the lands and moneys come to the Indians.
I would like to discuss the importance of Indian relations today in Canada. We are at a crossroads. I would be very concerned if the Government persisted in bringing in legislation, whether pertaining to self-government, compensation for comprehensive claims or whatever, and came running into the House with a sense of urgency with every Bill it might bring foward having to do with Indian affairs. The constitutional talks are going on right now. The Government has been using a ploy which I think is very unfair and which I would like to deny at this time. The Government is warning the aboriginal people of the country that if the Progressive Conservative Party gets elected as the Government of Canada the Indians
Lands Settlement Act
will be in far worse shape than they are now because we will ignore their affairs. Nothing is further from the truth. I categorically deny that today. My colleagues and my Leader categorically deny that. Our interest is in our aboriginal people, as I hope everybody in the House is interested in our aboriginal people. Our interest is to do what is absolutely the best for them and, in consultation with them, arrive at solutions that make good sense and are in favour of the aboriginal people of this country.
I would urge Members from the Government side of the House not to spread these fears throughout the aboriginal community because that is very unfair. The aboriginal people will become pawns in a political game which is completely uncalled for. The non-partisanship should be very strong when dealing with our aboriginal people. I caution the Government against taking a tactic like that, which they have been doing and which I have had drawn to my attention from many quarters, including The Fifth Estate. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to take the message to the Government that this Party supports aboriginal rights and the aboriginal people and will continue the process of carrying out what is best for them.
The constitutional talks which are going on right now are dragging a little bit. I attended all of them and found them interesting but rather frustrating. The federal Government is not in fact expressing a position but sitting back and listening to everyone else. This is a bit of a disappointment. I am hopeful that within the next couple of weeks at the First Ministers' conference regarding aboriginal rights on March 8 and 9 there will be something forthcoming that all the parties involved in the debate can sink their teeth into to begin a meaningful dialogue. I underline the word meaningful. This will be to the betterment of the aboriginal people.
I say to the Parliamentary Secretary, through you, Mr. Speaker, that her Marjesty's Loyal Opposition supports this Bill. We will assure that it gets through the three readings today. I was somewhat surprised that the Parliamentary Secretary did not take the opportunity to refer the Bill to the Committee of the Whole today as opposed to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. However, I may have missed it and we may come across that a little later on in debate.
Many Members of Her Majesty's Official Opposition will be speaking on this Bill today because it concerns them and they do have interest in it. In no way, shape or form is that to be interpreted as holding this Bill up because we will proceed with it today.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this very important Bill. It is an important Bill for the Indian people of British Columbia and for all British Columbians. I would first like to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) for the Bill and for the progress it symbolizes in correcting some longstanding injustice. It is not often I have an opportunity to

February 17, 1984
Lands Settlement Act
congratulate the Minister and I am very glad to be able to give credit where credit is due.
Progress in land claim settlements across Canada has been painfully slow. This is especially true in British Columbia. It is much slower than I want to see. Presumably it is slower than what the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would like to see, and certainly it is much slower than the Indian people would like to see. This Bill and the agreements which have led to it indicate some progress. I believe that the Minister deserves some credit for this. I believe that credit should also be given to the Government of British Columbia for finally making some progress on this one aspect of specific land claims.
Bill C-18 approves agreements involving the federal Government, the provincial Government of British Columbia and certain Indian bands in British Columbia which have had reserve lands taken from them as a result of the McKenna-McBride Commission, which held hearings between 1913 and 1916. Where agreements with the bands for compensation or return of lands have not yet been reached, the Bill provides for approval by the Governor in Council. Basically, Mr. Speaker, this Bill allows the federal Government to pay funds which have been negotiated with the Indian bands as part of the federal share of compensation.
It is important to note that the cut-off lands issue is separate from the related but larger issue of aboriginal land claims in British Columbia. It is time the Government of British Columbia recognized the validity of these claims and entered into serious negotiations. In this connection I would like to emphasize the importance of Clause 7 which was an important addition to the draft legislation tabled last June. Clause 7 provides:
Nothing in this Act affects any claims asserted by a band or the council of the band other than claims in respect of cut-off lands.
There were many Indian bands which were rather fearful of the agreements and earlier legislation which did not have this kind of clause. They were afraid that entering into an agreement of the cut-off lands would prejudice their case as far as the larger aboriginal claims which most of the Indian bands in British Columbia are asserting at the present time. Cut-off lands refer to those lands which had once been reserves and were cut off by various government actions. It is important to note that the McKenna-McBride Commission cut-offs were not the first and not the last of such cut-offs. They were the most blatant sign of high-handed government action that ignored the basic rights and wishes of the Indian people. It was also a very blatant indication of collusion between the provincial government and the federal Government at that time.
The history of Indian reserves in British Columbia has not been a happy one. At the beginning, the Indian people had all of the land. Aboriginal title in British Columbia is still something that they assert to the total area. They had well defined territories and there were clear divisions among the different Indian nations of British Columbia.
Settlement began on Vancouver Island under the auspices of the Hudson's Bay Company and the chief factor, Sir James Douglas. He later became Governor of the Crown colony of Vancouver Island, the sister colony of British Columbia, and finally the united colony of British Columbia. He negotiated some treaties with some of the Indian peoples around Victoria and Nanaimo. These treaties implicitly recognized the rights of Indian people to their land and they were, in a sense, negotiations for the use of resources to which the Indian people had valid claim.
Later, as governor of both Vancouver Island and British Columbia and then of the united colony, Governor Douglas ordered that reserves be set aside in accordance with the wishes of the Indian people themselves. That is, that the size of these reserves was not to be dictated by government but rather that the needs of the Indian people were to be met. These reserves were not to be reduced either by encroachment of settlers or by legislative action. In retrospect, Governor Douglas had a fairly generous policy.
However, in 1865, after the era of Governor Douglas had ended, Joseph Trutch became the new commissioner of lands and later became lieutenant-governor. Under his leadership a much different policy was adopted. The British Columbia Government refused to recognize aboriginal title and it reduced the size of the reserves that had been set up by Governor Douglas and which he said should not be encroached upon. It prohibited Indian people from buying land outside the reserve and discriminated against Indian people in the development or use of Crown land.
All of this was in spite of vigorous protests on the part of Indian people. Indian people in British Columbia have fought vigorously against government and non-governmental attempts to take away their rights. This is true of Indian people right across Canada. While the Indian movement is not simply something that has grown up in the last 10 or 15 years, the significance of the last few years has been the new sense of unity that is growing. It is still a fragile unity but Indian people have always tried to assert their rights.
Between 1876 and 1910 there was a federal-provincial Indian reserve commission. The job of that commission was to review the size of the reserves, some of which had been cut back by Mr. Trutch, and to establish new reserves in areas where they had not been set up. Sometimes reserves were enlarged and sometimes they were diminished.
The consultation that was supposed to take place with Indian bands was often very haphazard. After the commission had established new reserves, the very reactionary governments that existed in British Columbia at that time did not always recognize or approve these new reserves. This meant that the Indian people, even after they had a commission that recommended an enlarged reserve, could not always get the concurrence of the provincial government. There were continual hassles between the federal and provincial governments about the size of the reserve and the generosity of reserves.
February 17, 1984

Generally speaking, the reserves in British Columbia are only a fraction of the size of reserves in other parts of Canada.
Finally, an agreement was reached between the federal representative, Mr. McKenna, and the provincial premier, Sir Richard McBride, on September 24, 1912. They established a commission which was to tour throughout British Columbia and meet with Indian bands. According to Section 2 of the agreement that was reached on September 24, 1912, the commission had power to adjust the acreage of Indian reserves in British Columbia in the following manner:
(a)	At such places as the Commissioners are satisfied that more land is included in any particular Reserve as now defined than is reasonably required for the use of the Indians of that tribe or locality, the Reserve shall, with the consent of the Indians, as required by the Indian Act, be reduced to such acreage as the Commissioners think reasonably sufficient for the purposes of such Indians.
(b)	At any place at which the Commissioners shall determine that an insufficient quantity of land has been set aside for the use of Indians of that locality, the Commissioners shall fix the quantity that ought to be added for the use of such Indians. And they may set aside land for any Band of Indians for whom land has not already been reserved.
It is important to note in those terms of reference that any land that was to be reduced had to have the consent of the Indian people and that this was in accordance with the Indian Act itself.
As the commission travelled throughout British Columbia, the Indian people were assured that no action would be taken without their consent. But this assurance meant absolutely nothing. Some 36,000 acres were taken from 22 Bands absolutely without their consent and indeed over their strong and vigorous protests.
In 1920 the federal Government ratified this action by passing The British Columbia Indian Lands Settlement Act. Since Section 3 of that Act is instructive for our purposes this afternoon, I would like to read it:
For the purpose of adjusting, readjusting or confirming the reductions or cutoffs from reserves in accordance with the recommendations of the Royal Commission, the Governor in Council may order such reductions or cutoffs to be effected without surrenders of the same by the Indians, notwithstanding any provisions of the Indian Act to the contrary-
This is important when we get to Clause 4 of Bill C-18. Clause 4 reads:
4. Negotiations toward an agreement described in subsection 3(1), whether or not those negotiations result in such an agreement, do not constitute an admission by Her Majesty in right of Canada of the existence of any legal obligation of Her Majesty in right of Canada toward the band in question.
In other words, it was all done very legally. The Indian people were robbed of their lands by an Act that was passed by Parliament. That is legal as far as Bill C-18 is concerned and I suppose as far as the law of Canada is concerned, but it is not moral or just. Indian people have never accepted it. It has left a legacy of distrust so that when any of us, whether on the Liberal side or the Opposition side, speak to Indian people about legislation that might protect their rights, they are very rightly skeptical. The Indian Act contains many restrictions that have hampered their development over the years but also has built-in protection so that their lands could not be surrendered without their consent. The Indian people have seen how much that protection has meant once Parliament decided to
Lands Settlement Act
take away that right. The 1920 Act simply removed their right to vote on a surrender of lands and took it from them.
In addition to the official cut-offs following the McKenna-McBride Commission, the Ditchburn-Clark Commission was to review the recommendations of McKenna-McBride. Again, the Indian people were robbed of additional lands and resources.

Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was referring to the McKenna-McBride Commission which had the job of reviewing the findings of the Ditchburn-Clark Commission. I pointed out that in additional cases Indian people had land taken away from them. In addition to St. Mary's No. 1, the McKenna-McBride Commission allotted 1,280 acres to be designated as Indian Reverve No. 1A. Ditchburn-Clark nullified this and the reserve was never confirmed.
With regard to the Kitimat Indian Band, the McBride Commission ordered a ten-acre reserve cut-off. Ditchburn-Clark amended this by recommending that it be considered a "disallowed application", not a cut-off. That means that the Kitimat people are not eligible under the terms of this Bill or the federal-provincial agreement to have a claim for the cut-offs. In addition, we have the situation of the Lower Kootenay Band. It had a temporary reserve granted, which was kind of a funny status, before the McKenna-McBride Commission appeared.
I referred earlier to Section 2(b) of the terms of reference of the McKenna-McBride Commission which had the power to recommend enlargement of reserves. They did this. They issued an interim report No. 80 recommending additional lands. The final report of the McKenna-McBride Commission completely ignored this and in fact cut off 2,370 acres from the Lower Kootenay Band, leaving it with only 365 acres.
The Lower Kootenay Band at present is accusing the McKenna-McBride Commission of a form of fraud. They have submitted a specific claim which does not come under the terms of the cut-off lands legislation. Nevertheless, we can get some idea of the way in which some of the commissioners operated not in the interest of the Indian people. I quote from page 28 of the Lower Columbia submission:
On May 13, 1915 Royal Commissioner D. M. MacDowell wrote to Guy Lowenberg in Creston "P.S. Confidentially I can tell you that in dealing with the Creston Reserves we have not neglected your reclamation interests, and no doubt when you are ready to begin work you will be able to ascertain this through the Prov. Govt."
The Ditchburn-Clark Commission continued the process of whittling away at Indian reserves. The final transfer of Indian reserves to the federal Government in trust was not completed until 1938 when Order in Council 1036 was passed. Even that Order in Council reserved to the provincial government the power to expropriate up to one-twentieth of the land of any Indian reserves for highways, pipelines, utility lines, railroads or what have you, without compensation. The McKenna-McBride cut-offs have to be seen in the context of a long history of stealing Indian land by the Governments of Canada and British Columbia.
The movement toward the settlement of the McKenna-McBride cut-offs began in 1969 when the federal Government agreed to negotiate. In 1975 the British Columbia Government under Premier Dave Barrett agreed to negotiate. I am pleased that it was an NDP Government in Canada that Finally began
the process, but it has to be acknowledged that even that government did not come easily to this position.
I remember a large demonstration in the early summer of 1975 where Indian people were presenting their case to the NDP Government. I remember people going to the NDP convention that year and making a very strong case. They made the case to the rank and file membership of the New Democratic Party and they adopted convention policy that eventually led to the Government's change of policy. That is a heartening example of democracy at work. The Indian people recognize that there is a great deal of goodwill out there if they can only be heard and have their case made.
I want to make a few remarks about the principles of settlement. The money for this settlement comes out of the public purse. There are situations where land was taken from Indian bands and sold to private interests, yet the money for the settlement comes from the public purse. There is no displacement of individual residents. This is important. It indicates that the Government has acted in their interests as well as in the interests of the Indian people in this settlement. It is an important principle to remember when we consider other settlements, especially those relating to offshore rights of fisheries that are involved in some of the aboriginal claims presently accepted for negotiation in British Columbia.
We want to see full justice for the Indian people. It has to be paid for by all the people of Canada rather than just narrow segments. That refers specifically to the fact that an increased Indian participation in the fishery should not be solely at the expense of other British Columbia fishermen. The money involved in this settlement is not an overgenerous sum when you consider the loss of land involved.
I want to emphasize that this money has to be in addition to other moneys that would normally go to Indian bands in British Columbia. There are very disturbing indications that as the Government moves toward what it calls Indian self-government and gives Indian bands greater control, it is cutting off some other very important services. For example, the Urban Native Society of Vancouver has been involved in training urban Indian people in Vancouver over the last 20 years. The funding it received from the federal Government is being cut off.
This shucking off of responsibility and claiming that the bands have the authority to act is not good enough. Conditions have to be improved on the reserves so that people are not squeezed out of them and into the crowded downtown cores of our cities. In the meantime, we have to continue providing some help for those who do go to our cities. Consider a report by the Vancouver Native Peace Liaison Committee which estimates there are some 6,000 native Indian people in Vancouver. The federal Government is doing nothing to help them.
The agreements which have been reached with Indian bands are not perfect. There are assertions in the agreements of provincial title without a recognition of aboriginal title. This is offensive to the Indian people. The present provincial government is playing a very negative role in reaching settlements in the larger aboriginal claims.
February 17, 1984

Before we get too self-congratulatory on what we have been able to achieve in the cut-off claims, perhaps we should place this once again in the larger context of aboriginal claims. I will conclude by quoting a statement by Mr. Charles Wesley, a band spokesman for the Kispaiox people, when he appeared before the McKenna-McBride Commission in April, 1915. He said, and I quote:
I wish to tell you that this reserve that you have just spoken about is something that we don't wish for, for this reason; We don't want a reserve. This country originally belonged to our ancestors ... and it is only quite recently that the Government sent men out here to measure this land immediately around us, and we were not notified of it when they did it; then the Provincial Government came in and sold the remaining land immediately around us. All the old camps up the Kispaiox river, where we used to gather our salmon, and our hunting camps, and where we used to pick berries, and what we most strenuously object to is that you insist upon us having this reserve. You have measured all these reserves and you say that that is yours-
We asked that the land which the Provincial Government had sold be returned or given back to us. The Bible is placed between us that we all act true-you gentlemen to speak the truth, the Interpreter to speak the truth, and I will speak the truth. We see it written . .. that the word of God is that a man is not to move another man's landmark. The land marked off for our ancestors was from mountain to mountain, and this is what the Government has picked up into small pieces. This is where our inheritances came from and where they were handed down from generation to generation, but now these have all been sold; therefore we ask that these be returned.
I am glad the Government has been able to negotiate with some of the bands for cut-off lands settlements and that the Government of British Columbia has participated in it. I welcome this Bill. I hope similar satisfactory agreements will be reached with other bands. I also urge upon the federal Government, and especially upon the provincial government, to get on with the act of negotiating and settling the larger and more basic aboriginal claims which Indian people have submitted and which, in the opinion of our Party, are very just.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few brief moments to add some comments to this debate. We on this side of the House have been very instrumental and active in helping to facilitate the discussions which are culminating here today, namely, the ratification by Parliament of the understanding reached among the Province of British Columbia, the Government of Canada and the Indian people affected by the B.C. cut-off lands question.
Some of my colleagues have already participated in this matter. Those who follow will talk about the history of this long outstanding question. The Province of British Columbia was never very satisfied with the conditions attached to the agreement to join Confederation, particularly with regard to Indian lands. If one researches the debates and the discussions in British Columbia from the time B.C. joined Confederation until the McKenna-McBride Commission was appointed, one will find that the debates with regard to this question were always acrimonious and bitter. Many people felt that the Indians were treated too generously and that the reserves, the land set aside for them, were in the way of development in the B.C. region. Of course, today all of us have a much more
Lands Settlement Act
enlightened view about that, and it is today that we are attempting to redress some of the injustices of the past-the deliberate deceptions which we have perpetrated upon our Indian brothers and sisters, the injury of contracts into which we have entered with them, and the treaties and conventions which exist between us.
Basically the settlement is designed either to restore land affected by the cut-off provisions or, in cases where land has been alienated to the point where it can no longer be returned to Indian people, to have the two senior governments enter into an agreement and arrive at a formula whereby they would be compensated for that land either by an exchange or cash payments.
I would like to refer to one example of a particular cut-off question. It concerns the Penticton Band and an agreement which is one of the three or four that are fully negotiated. The reserve area involved was about 14,000 acres. The area alienated was 12,000 acres. There is a federal contribution of $13,217,000 and a provincial contribution of $1 million to this particular band. It is one of the larger ones, if not the largest. Not all of them are that significant, but this example gives an idea of how significant and serious the injustices have been which we have perpetrated upon the Indians of British Columbia in the past.
Of course, one has to understand that the situation in British Columbia is a unique one. There are treaties in B.C. Treaty No. 8 comes in from the east and takes in most, if not all, of the area east of the Rocky Mountains. The rest of the province is not covered by treaties, except for smaller ones in the lower mainland area. The remainder of the province has not been settled and treaties have not been negotiated. Some Indian people in the province claim that no settlements have ever been made, that no arrangements have ever been made, that indeed they have never selected any land and that all the land is up for negotiation.
Therefore we are pleased that it was possible to bring the three actors in this drama together and to arrive at an agreement, inadequate as it will obviously be, which will certainly put that question behind us. I am particularly pleased. I join with the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) in the assertion that, while this will put the cut-off land question behind us, it is certainly not to be seen as a solution to the larger, outstanding question of comprehensive claims and some specific claims which have yet to be settled in the province. I would prefer, as I always have, to have this long outstanding question dealt with in a very expeditious manner and as much as possible with the legitimate concerns, rights and aspirations of the Indian people in mind.
We are at a very critical time in our history as far as Indian people are concerned. We are at a crossroads. Much has happened over the last three or four years particularly, some of it brought on by the decision that we should have an entrenched Constitution and that we should patriate it. Of course, the question as to how our Indian people would be respected and recognized in the constitution had to be decided.

February 17, 1984
Lands Settlement Act
The decision could not be made before the actual patriation and entrenchment took place.
Therefore, the partners in the scheme, the provincial and federal governments, decided that a series of constitutional conferences should be held designed to resolve this particular problem. One such conference will be held next month. It will be the second in a series of these conferences. Indian people are very much engaged in the process of deciding themselves just what kind of role they should be playing in the future of our Confederation.
If one studies history and the proclamations, treaties, contracts and conventions that have existed since 1763 when the first one was signed, one cannot help but be sympathetic to the view of some Indians and their leaders in the country. They still hold that, considering the past, an effective way will never be found to permit them to join society in a participatory way that would help them regain their self-respect and allow them to pursue their legitimate aspirations for themselves and future generations. Those Indian leaders say to their brothers and sisters that the answer to their problem would be self-government outside the framework of confederation and the existing institutions in the country.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, with seven colleagues I participated in a two-year study of Indian self-government. We came to the conclusion, which I should like to think is supported by the majority of Indian people in the country, that a partial answer to redressing some of the past injustices would be to encourage them to join Canada as full citizens and in a way that would permit them to establish a distinct form of self-government which could be brought into the framework of Confederation. I will spend whatever time I have to work on this objective.
The committee of which I was a member and the report of which I was co-author suggest a way to bring about a kind of self-government structure which could function within the framework of Confederation. It would permit Indian people to begin the long, tedious process of recapturing their past, recovering their self-respect, rebuilding their economy and recapturing the soul they lost when the land was taken from them, and to build their culture. It can easily be seen that this would require a form of self-government that would exceed the powers of municipal governments and in some cases even the powers of provincial governments. It would mean that the Indian people would take charge and accept the responsibility that goes along with managing one's own affairs, planning the future of one's children and assuming control of one's life. The rest of us would have to make the necessary accommodations to make that possible.
The Bill is a small step in the long, tedious process in this long journey which we must all take together to remove the incredible shame that hangs over all Canadian society for the treatment of our Indian people over the last 300 years. This is not a perfect solution, but for those that are affected by the cut-off land question it would redress the injustice that was
particularly associated with the work of the McKenna-McBride Commission and the collusion of the provincial and federal governments at that time.
I am proud to be associated with passage of the Bill and since we want it to pass all stages today I will end my remarks at this point.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a few moments to put on record some of the problems that passage of Bill C-18 will leave with a good portion of my constituency. Let me preface my remarks by saying that I realize how long and hard these negotiations have been and what an hour this is for an injustice perpetrated in our history to be corrected.
In the riding of Capilano we have a very wealthy, very powerful, very skilled Indian band. Its leaders are as skilled in the art of politics as any group of people in the country. They are a source of pride to those of us who live around the Squamish Band reserve. They own properties through First Narrows on the north of Burrard Inlet all the way through to Lonsdale. They own very valuable real estate and are an extremely wealthy band, not only at present but potentially in the future.
The City of North Vancouver has no problem with the return of the cut-off land. I have spoken to the mayor and the council of the City of North Vancouver and they are happy that this is proceeding. The Corporation of the District of North Vancouver really has no problem other than the fact that we built our sewage plant on Indian cut-off lands and the District of North Vancouver, the Municipality of West Vancouver and the City of North Vancouver are subject to a whole new cost and arrangement for sewage flow. From correspondence I have had with the Corporation of the District of North Vancouver, I believe that the Greater Vancouver regional district and these municipalities have arranged something in the order of $70,000 initial lease rental on that plant. The surrounding municipalities and the Indian band and properties are very closely integrated in terms of service, bus, water, electricity, road access, building permits and all by-laws. There is now an interface that could cause some concern and anxiety to the municipalities.
The municipality in the riding of Capilano that has cause for anxiety as a result of the cut-off land settlement is the Municipality of West Vancouver. In that municipality 25.9 acres, that is the parcel titled Lot 5521, make up soccer fields, a pitch and putt golf course, the beach, the playground-it really makes up a regional park that serves the Greater Vancouver district. The Municipality of West Vancouver has spent much money and talent over the years in developing this park. In addition, there is a wildlife refuge and some very attractive ponds.
This complete recreation area, this open expanse, when classified or appraised and assessed as park land, comes out at a value of $3 million and, when classified and assessed for
February 17, 1984

highest and best use in terms of high-rise development, comes out with a value of forty-odd million dollars. That kind of price differential has caused an element of friction between the Municipality of West Vancouver and the Indian band.
I can agree with the chiefs of the Indian bands-and I compliment them on their skills-when they say that they want the land returned, that they need to have it in their hands because it was taken from them by fraud. They want it in order to have the leverage to deal properly and more favourably with the Municipality of West Vancouver. Bill C-18 leaves a good part of the riding of Capilano with the prospect of a major set of negotiations in the future.
I want to see if, in my duties as a Member of Parliament, I can reduce the tensions of that interface as we come into the next few years. For instance, the municipality has a no sign bylaw. On the Indian lands, which surround the entrance to the Lions Gate bridge, one can imagine the value of neon signs, billboards and so on. So this kind of interface with the municipalities is a potential source of trouble. As well the municipalities provide the access, the services, much of the water and everything else for the Indian band, and it is because of this leverage, this teeter-totter of new bargaining position which the Squamish Indian Band has picked up, that we are going to have a most interesting period, particularly for those politicians who serve the Municipality of West Vancouver.
I will not relate the history, nor the justice which is being done in the passage of Bill C-18, Mr. Speaker. I believe the speakers on behalf of the Government and the critics from the Progressive Conservative Party and New Democratic Party have covered that aspect of the Bill. I am going to hold my few remarks to some of the problems and make a plea to both the Indian band in Capilano and the Municipality of West Vancouver to enter into high-level negotiations with the spirit of co-operation, rather than have a long, lengthy period of confrontation which will create tensions and unnecessary anxieties in the future.
Something else which complicates that situation in Capilano, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that back in 1972 an upstart candidate came along and decided to run against the Fisheries Minister of the Liberal Government. That Fisheries Minister had something like a majority of 28,800. Anyone who would consider running against that very talented, very well educated Rhodes scholar who served the Liberal Party, had to be nuts and had to be defeated. I did a pretty good job of cutting his majority down. My goodness, Mr. Speaker, what a cost the people of Canada have paid ever since.
During the 1972 election the Government was throwing money around as only Liberals can.

speechtext:
The year 1972 was the shade of things to come because this Minister of Fisheries decided that he would move all the West Coast environmental and fisheries offices
Lands Settlement Act
into a location on the waterfront in First Narrows on the Indian reserve. And we have been paying an annual adjusted cost rental on that vacant property-which still has the same bullrushes and swamp grass it had in 1972-of $6.7 million to the Indian band for that political promise of the then Minister of Fisheries. We have been living with this for a long time, Mr. Speaker. About two or three years ago, the solicitor for the Indian band approached its Member of Parliament and asked if he would assist in having the federal Government co-ordinate all the potential public works projects for final development on that land which we have been paying so dearly for. We started into very quiet negotiations. I agreed automatically to keep it out of the political realm and see what would come to pass. Well, some three years have passed. A couple of Senators took the project over, I was no longer consulted and so nothing has happened. We do hear rumours that the fisheries station at Caulfield, which is also in my riding, is about to receive a magnificent permanent dwelling. The Department of Fisheries out there has a bricks and mortar complex, you must remember, Mr. Speaker, not protection of the species or the environment.
I suggest that instead of building that plant at Caulfield, it should be built on the very expensive land we have leased for the next 60 or 70 years. That is what the original agreement stated and the Indians are not going to accept anything less unless there are some major tradeoffs which would give them great advantage. Those Indians signed a lease with the federal Government which said that the Department of Fisheries and the Department of the Environment will locate structures on that land. The Indians agreed to this lease not just for the money, but because they saw it as an opportunity to attract other activities of a high standard and order to that centre so that the whole value of their surrounding lands would be enhanced.
We are very proud of the political and business acumen of the Indian leaders in my riding. They can outsmart us "honk-ies", or whatever one wants to call us, any time of the day. They have the time and patience which we do not. Money has been poured into the riding. Yet I feel the provincial government, in negotiating with the federal Government and with the Indian band, has really let the municipality and the residents of West Vancouver down because it did not consider the park land, the golf course and that whole recreational area. They are encumbered lands and those lands have now been returned to the Indian band. I suppose the Indians correctly and rightfully feel that the surrounding municipalities and residents have really been keeping the Indian lands as open space protection. We in West Vancouver do not know whether we are going to lose this beautiful park area, whether it is going to be covered with high-rise development or what.
I want to make a plea to these constituents and to the Indians, through the opportunity of this debate, to forget some of the things which have happened in the past. I believe officers of the municipality have been extremely rude and hard with Indian negotiators. I believe perhaps we in the outside municipality lack the negotiating skills which the Indian lead-

February 17, 1984
Lands Settlement Act
ers have. Perhaps we can improve our approach to these negotiations. If we do not do this willingly, I believe we are going to be forced to do so just through the economic axe, which we have a tendency to understand. I would like to see the Indian band and the Municipality of West Vancouver find the right vehicle in which to tie all these things together, such as the Department of the Environment lease on the Indian lands. Instead of building a permanent fisheries research establishment at Caulfield, perhaps that should be considered as one of the tradeoffs. Perhaps a compromise has to be made in terms of high-rise development on Lot 5521 vis-a-vis some of it remaining open for parks. Certainly, the Indians must benefit from that openness and the beauty of that setting.
We are debating second reading of Bill C-18 today. This Bill is something we are all pleased to have happen. However, I must say that it does leave at least one of the ridings in Canada with some very major problems ahead of it. I would hope that a new spirit of negotiation can be started which will resolve with a minimum of disturbance and tension some of the problems left.
I cannot help but say I object most strenuously to Bills coming in at the last minute and being passed in this House through all stages on a Friday afternoon. I believe it is travesty of the purpose and function of this House and Members of Parliament. I want to remind you, Sir, that the same thing happened with Bill C-169. It passed all stages on a Friday afternoon and we trampled on some essential rights and freedoms. Each and every one of us in this House should be ashamed of doing so. We have not corrected that travesty because we got lazy, we got impatient, we had a deadline set on a Bill just as we have a deadline on this Bill. I have transcripts of meetings and negotiations between the municipalities and the provincial government going way back into last year, saying this Bill would be passed last fall. Yet here we are with a deadline of March 6 for this Bill and we are rushing through the speeches.
As a Member of Parliament I object most strenuously to that, and on behalf of my constituents I want to take this opportunity to apologize, because it was only this morning that I learned about this Bill coming forward today. That is probably my fault, I should have known about it yesterday. I also apologize for what I have done to the rights of free people in allowing Bill C-169 to pass through in a similar manner.

they are, what they are like, what the temperature is there, and how much of a loss they were to the Indian bands. As I hope you know, the Okanagan is some 300 miles from the centre of "Lotus land", as some people call Vancouver.

That is God's country. It is also 300 miles from the City of Calgary, so it is in the very enviable position of being right at the centre of everything that is important in western Canada.
As you may well know, the lake starts at the American border and goes up some 70 miles to where it ends in the lands of the Okanagan Indian Band. Midway is the City of Kelowna, at the south end is the City of Penticton, and at the very north end is the City of Vernon. That lake is one of the most pristine and beautiful lakes in all of Canada. Many of these cut-off lands were taken directly next to the lake so they were very valuable indeed.
The climate in the Okanagan, as I hope everyone knows, is one of the most beautiful in the world. We have four distinct seasons: a gentle winter, nice spring, hot and dry summer, and a nice long fall. These conditions are ideal for growing the many crops we do. In fact, starting from the border up to Vernon and beyond is probably one of the best fruit-producing areas in all of Canada. We grow many crops there, many vegetables, and we also do a great deal of lumbering. These are the kinds of activities the Indian bands located in my constituency are involved in, and they do them exceedingly well.
We have industry there, non-polluting industries, and oddly enough manufacturing is a very high income producer in the Okanagan even though that area is now rather depressed.
Speaking of Okanagan Lake, I would be somewhat remiss if I failed to mention another very important aspect of that lake and to add perhaps a little light relief to this dry debate today. subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA INDIAN CUT-OFF LANDS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
They are all very good businessmen. In my constituency, Mr. Speaker, we have two Indian bands, one being the Spalluncheen Band. That band has some 320 members, its chief is Wayne Christian and the band manager is Graham Go. There are three reserves for this band: Salmon River reserve, the Enderby reserve and the Sicamous reserve. The band is primarily occupied with forestry, including logging, and agriculture, farming and livestock. It might be of interest to know that that band has built some 26 new homes on reserves over the past three years.
The band most closely connected with Bill C-18 is, of course, the Okanagan Indian Band. Its chief is Murray Alexis, and the Parliamentary Secretary in his closing remarks quoted Murray Alexis at the time he signed contracts approving of this particular Bill. There are five reserves in this band: the Okanagan Indian reserve where about 600 members of the band live. Since there are only 875 members in total, this is by far the largest reserve and it sits right at the top of Okanagan Lake. There is Otter Lake reserve, the Harris Lake reserve, the Priest Valley reserve and the Duke Lake Indian reserve which is near the town of Winfield. These reserves were established at the time of the Indian settlements at the turn of the century, especially at the north end of the lakes where rivers and creeks provided the only means of transportation.
The Okanagan Indian Band is known for its independence of spirit. These Indians know and value their land. They have established many industries and farm communities. They have established good orchards, small market gardens and are highly responsible and independent. We in the Okanagan are very proud and pleased that they are part of our community. One of the great statesmen of that period was Chief Nichola, an Indian chief renowned throughout British Columbia for his wisdom and his skills in agriculture. In recognition of his leadership, he lies buried in honour at the head of Okanagan Lake. Some 35 new homes were placed in that band last year. By and large I would say they are a model for Indian bands throughout British Columbia.
Lands Settlement Act
I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak to Bill C-18. We in the Okanagan do not have the conflict which the Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) is faced with in his community. I am very happy with that. I can see he does have some difficulties. I am sure if they in that community use the wisdom and prudence which the Member has displayed on many occasions in the House they will resolve their problems very adequately. The Okanagan Indian Band is one of the 22 Indian bands whose original reserves were reduced in size without Indian consent. Much of that has been detailed in the House this afternoon.
I will describe the events in the Okanagan. As a result of the McKenna-McBride Commission of 1916 an area comprising 51.82 hectares of land was cut away from Long Lake Indian Reserve No. 5. The House might like to know that Long Lake is not now the Okanagan Lake, although that is what it should be. It is now called Lake Kalamalka, the lake of many colours. We do not dump any sewage into Kalamalka Lake that I am aware of. I live on the lake and I drink the water as it comes from the lake, as does everyone else around the lake, and we are all very healthy. We have very pristine, potable water in the Okanagan. It is probably one of the few places in the world where there is such pure water.
That was very valuable land which the Okanagan Indian Band lost. In 1983 the Government of Canada finally agreed to pay compensation of $1.4 million to the band for lands cut off which are no longer available to be returned. Subject to ratification by the band, the Province of British Columbia will return some 27.4 hectares of land and will pay $32,500 in full compensation of that claim.
We have been asked by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) to pass this Bill speedily in order to enable the federal Government to meet its responsibility, and in order that the provincial Government meet its responsibility and act under the agreement. I would not normally pay much attention to the Minister's request that we hurry this Bill through. I received a letter from Chief Murray Alexis written June 23, 1983. It reads in part as follows:
We have reviewed the proposed legislation and have consulted our legal advisor to determine if the proposed legislation should be of concern to us. The Council has been advised that the legislation is in order and that it would be in the Band's best interest if it were passed without delay.
He goes on to say:

The view of history held today by most non-Indian Canadians and the perspective held by most Indian people are almost mirror images. Indian people consider the "discoverers" and "explorers", in whose memory monuments are erected and postage stamps issued, to have been intruders in a land already well known to the nations that inhabited it. Indian people know their nations to have been productive, cultured, spiritual, intelligent civilizations comparable to those in Europe at the time of first contact. But they are portrayed instead as savages and pagans, unknowing of religion and needing instruction in simple tasks.
