Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned, this Bill has had a long and bitter history. The negotiations that led to this tripartite agreement have their roots back in the nineteenth century. British Columbia entered Confederation in 1871. The federal Government inherited the responsibility for the Indians and Indian lands. It is at this time that the federal-provincial disputes over Indian affairs arose.
The 13th article of the Terms of Union provided that:
(1)	The charge of the Indians and the trusteeship and management of the lands reserved for their use and benefit shall be assumed by the Dominion Government.
(2)	A policy as liberal as that hitherto pursued by the B.C. Government shall be continued by the Dominion Government after the Union.
(3)	To carry out such policy, tracts of land of such extent as it has hitherto been the practice of the B.C. Government to appropriate-
-for Indians-
-shall from time to time be conveyed by the local government to the Dominion Government in trust for the use and benefit of the Indians.
That was in 1871, and there has been a dispute for the last 111 years.
An important argument in this dispute was the difference between the two Governments about the basis of allotting acreage on reserves. The federal Government proposed 80 acres be allotted to each family. The province claimed that 10 acres per family was enough, and kept I. W. Powell from allotting acreage and surveying any additional reserves. It is important to realize the importance of that particular formula because our forefathers were dealing in acreage at a time when we know that the Indian people were involved in agrology,
February 17, 1984

fishing and living off the land. Land has increased in value ten thousand-fold since that time.
The point I am making is that if we let this fact elude us, we will continue to delay legitimate Indian claims. At the time of the settlement, the increase in the value of the land would be a direct and additional heavy burden on the taxpayers of Canada. That is why it is a shame that the federal Government and the provincial Government in British Columbia have delayed settlement of these particular claims.
I referred to I. W. Powell. Mr. Powell said at the time of the First negotiations that, "If there has not been an Indian war, it is not because there has been no injustice to the Indians but because the Indians have not been sufficiently united". As my colleague and friend from Capilano has stated, there is indeed unity among the Indian bands in British Columbia at the present time. As he also said, they have both the time and the moxie to outclass us in negotiations. It is time that we respected that ability, that sincerity and that right which they do indeed have in these particular claims.
The impasse between the federal and provincial Governments continued through the late 1900s and into this century. In 1911, this dispute reached a head. Essentially, British Columbia never wanted to give the federal Government juris-dication over Indian lands. In 1911 there was an attempt to resolve the dispute by referring it to the Supreme Court of Canada. But at that juncture the Province of British Columbia backed down. The province in its own right then passed legislation giving itself the authority to "grant, convey, quit claim, sell or dispose of . . . on such terms as may be deemed advisable . . . the interest of the province . . . reversionary or otherwise ... in any Indian reserve or any portion thereof'. The unilateral attitude behind that legislation is a problem.
The province's law was a direct challenge to the federal Government and indeed to the Indian people. The result of these negotiations was the McKenna-McBridge Agreement in 1912. The history of that agreement has been well covered during this brief debate. Although I have researched it, I need not go through it again at this time.
According to the agreement which the commission had reached, legal title to the cut-off lands remained with the province, with the requirement that the province turn over to the bands 50 per cent of the proceeds realized from the sale or other disposition of the lands.
Obviously the bands involved felt that there was a breach of the McKenna-McBride Agreement because lands were cut off without their consent by reason of the provincial legislation. The grievance of the Indians over cut-off lands has persisted throughout the years. Both levels of Government were pressed for retribution for the cut-off lands.
In 1969 the federal Government agreed to negotiate a settlement of the grievance. Successive federal Ministers of Indian Affairs have publicly supported the need to redress Indian bands for cut-off lands. Negotiations between the two Governments and a committee representing the bands began in 1977.
Lands Settlement Act
Today we are dealing with a long-standing claim by 22 Indian bands in British Columbia that had 33,400 acres of land taken from 34 reserves some 60 years old without their consent. It is for this reason that we are here today finally to receive this Bill for second and third reading and final passage. I am pleased to have had this opportunity to speak to Bill C-18. It is a good thing that we will shortly see the passage of this legislation, for without it the provincial Government will not be obliged to transfer lands or money to any of the 22 cut-off bands.

When you read through the Bill, you find that is not the case. Apparently the Minister already has authority to enter into agreements of this nature. The parties who do not have that authority and to whom it must be given by Parliament are the bands and the band councils.
It is the intention of Clause 3 of the Bill to give to a band council the authority to enter into these agreements. This is indicative of several problems that are faced by bands and band councils throughout Canada. Under the Indian Act, they do not have authority to enter into legally binding agreements. This prohibition frequently delays considerably the needed developments on reserves that have been set aside. The inability to enter into legally binding contracts such as mortgages makes it very difficult for such developments to take place.
I can well understand the frustration that band councils must feel when they have good deals going, when they want to take advantage of the land on the reserves or other resources such as lumber contained thereon, and they find themselves prevented from entering into mortgages and similar types of arrangements with which to raise the necessary funds. Under the Indian Act they are denied that authority, which comes as a matter of course to practically any other body corporate in Canada. What we are doing with this Bill is giving that needed authority.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reducing the cost burden on Canadian farmers by removing the 9 per cent federal sales tax on diesel fuel and gasoline used for the production of food.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I genuinely apppreciate the opportunity to present this motion at this time because I feel it is very timely. It is timely because it comes on the heels of the Budget, which was introduced this week, which really provides no relief whatsoever for the agricultural community and specifically the individual farmer who has been faced with some very difficult problems. The Budget fails to address any of the problems which are facing individual farmers in the agricultural community as a whole, and it even goes beyond that and fails to acknowledge that there are serious problems.
I feel this motion is timely also in that this debate happens to take place roughly on the fourth anniversary of the Liberal Party's return to power. We all know what the platform of the Liberal Party was during the course of that election campaign. It was basically a platform based on deceit, subterfuge and quite frankly, a hidden agenda. While the members of the Liberal Party talked about a "made in Canada" energy price, they certainly did not spell it out in any detail. They misled the Canadian public into believing that energy prices would be lower than those proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party.
Farmers are now contemplating their planting. They are seriously considering what they are going to seed and how much. Given the fact that the commodity prices are low, input costs are high, and there is no relief in the Budget, it is a time

February 17, 1984

when farmers are seriously looking at their future in terms of what sort of production patterns they can contemplate. I believe, for those three reasons, it is a very timely subject.
I would like to reiterate once again, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada are in very serious financial difficulty. This measure would provide some relief. It would serve to alleviate their problems somewhat-not much, but somewhat. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his Budget speech talked about the need for confidence, hope and optimism, and the need to increase productivity and our competitive position. I listened very intently to those words, Mr. Speaker, but there is really nothing in this Budget which relates to improving the confidence, hope and optimism of the agricultural community of Canada. Therefore, I believe this motion should be given very serious consideration.
Let us just look briefly over the last four years to see what has happened in the agricultural community. In the last four years there have been close to 2,000 farm bankruptcies. That is a huge number, and all the bankruptcies or farm failures are not recorded. That figure of 2,000 bankruptcies does not clearly identify those who have voluntarily gone out of business or those who have gone into receivership and are not a statistic. There were 488 farmers who declared bankruptcy in the year 1983. That is almost 400 per cent more farm bankruptcies than occurred in 1979. Roughly 125 bankruptcies were registered in 1979. In 1983 there were 488. For example, in western Canada, there was a doubling of the figure for 1982. Why has this occurred? Primarily, Mr. Speaker, it has happened for reasons beyond the individual farmer's control. It is not because farmers have not been productive. It is not because they have not been good managers. It is basically because of developments which are quite clearly beyond their control, such as low commodity prices and high input costs, and it is largely as a result of the policies of the Government.
There are two very important elements to that component, Mr. Speaker. The first is the interest rate policy of the Government, and the second is the energy pricing policy. There is no explanation for this Government's current energy pricing policy. It really constitutes the largest revenue grab by a federal Government in the history of this country, and it is a revenue grab which has been carried out on the backs of the food producers. We know, in terms of our food component in this society, we still have one of the lowest food components of any industrialized nation in the world. I do not believe the farmer should be further hampered and strapped with this additional cost simply to feed the coffers of the federal Government.
We all remember the campaign of 1980 and the Liberal promise to keep energy prices low. The Liberals did not say how low, but they certainly did not tell the Canadian people that the prices were going to rise to the heights at which they are today. Let me review what has happened over the four-year period. I phoned the Gulf dealer in the Town of Two Hills, Alberta, earlier this afternoon. I asked him to compare the prices of farm fuel today with prices which were in effect four years ago today. In February, 1980, gasoline used for
Agriculture
farm production purposes cost 72.96 cents per gallon. At the same time, diesel fuel cost 65.68 cents a gallon. Today, in February, 1984, the price of gasoline used on the farm for food production purposes is $1.45 per gallon. That includes a 32-cent provincial tax reduction which occurred in 1982. Therefore, if the provincial tax had remained in effect, as it was in 1980, it would have added another 32 cents and would have brought the price up to $1.77 per gallon. In the case of diesel fuel, the price today is $1.37. Here again that includes a 32-cent provincial tax reduction which took place in 1982. So even taking that into consideration, there is a doubling of the fuel prices in that four-year period. We all know what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said on January 31, 1980, in Alvinston, Ontario. He said this:
Farmers and consumers will get a break from the federal Liberal agriculture policy-
Farmer costs of production will be held in check and as a result so will consumer prices-
Fuels used in farm production will be exempt from any excise tax and a special price structure established.
Basically, Mr. Speaker, we are asking this Government and particularly the Minister of Agriculture, to fulfil at least part of that promise he made back in January 1980. Failure to do so would be an outright betrayal. The removal of the 9 per cent sales tax on diesel fuel and gasoline used for the production of food would reduce the price of fuel by roughly 17 cents or 18 cents. It is a rather interesting figure. I could say that if you included the removal of the Canadian ownership charge- which has fulfilled its obligation-of 4.5 cents a gallon, we could have a saving of 22.5 cents a gallon for the producer. That would help. The federal tax component on farm fuels is roughly 30 per cent to 40 per cent of the pump price. For every gallon of gas or fuel sold, about 62 cents go into the federal Government coffers. This is costing Canadian farmers roughly $275 million a year. In 1981, farmers spent $1.2 billion for energy. In addition, they spent $600 million to $700 million for fertilizer, including an energy tax component of probably 10 per cent. If you look at fuel taxes alone, they constitute 20 per cent of all energy costs. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say this is not an unreasonable proposition.
Prairie farmers paid an average of $5,100 in direct energy costs in 1981. This contributes immensely to farm input costs and the cost-price squeeze. We note that farm input costs have tripled since 1971. Since the beginning of 1980 they have gone up by 35 per cent. In the meantime, the selling price of the farmers' products is basically at the same level. If you use the price deflator, you will find commodity prices below the level of 1972-73.
The price of grain, Mr. Speaker, is a good example of what I have been saying. The producer price at the ports of Thunder Bay or Vancouver in the 1979-80 crop year was $196.43 per metric tonne. Today, including the final payment for 1982-83, the net realized price was $192.34. I should not say "the net realized price". That was the net price at the point of departure. Therefore, grain prices have fallen over the last four

February 17, 1984
Agriculture
years. There really is not much control over that because in order to sell our grain abroad we must be competitive. However, we have a Government which has imposed horrendous taxes on the backs of the producer. This year it increased freight rates. My proposal would at least lessen some of this impact. I urge the Government to seriously consider this because it is important for the farmers of Canada to have some faith and confidence, some degree of optimism.
I could go on and give you all sorts of figures on net income, Mr. Speaker. As recorded by Statistics Canada, farmers are making about 50 per cent of what they made in 1975. That is hardly cause for joy or optimism. Other countries support their producers to a greater extent than Canada. Fuel prices in other countries are much lower. U.S. fuel prices are roughtly 20 per cent to 25 per cent below the prices Canadian farmers are paying. The ten-year average support paid to farmers per metric tonne was $6.35 for wheat in Canada, $11.41 in the United States and $19.96 in the EEC. For barley producers in Canada, assistance was largely in the form of the cheap freight rate, the Crowsnest Pass freight rate which has now gone down the tube. Canadian producers were supported to the tune of $6.32 per ton, U.S. producers received $7.57, and the EEC it was $32.80 per ton. That gives you an idea of what competing countries do for their producers. We call upon this Government to recognize that and take some steps to ensure that we do our part to ensure Canadian producers are indeed competitive. Agriculture is and will continue in the foreseeable future to be a major component of Canada's economy.
I noted from The Globe and Mail that last year alone, Mr. Speaker, the farm program in the U.S. cost the federal Treasury some $28 billion. They are supporting their farmers, but Canada is not supporting its farmers commensurate with producers in other countries. When you consider the importance of agriculture, you realize it makes up about 40 per cent of the nation's economy. While roughly 5 per cent of the population is directly involved in the production of food, the agri-food system employs about 18 per cent of the Canadian work force. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there are many reasons for the Government to look at this motion very seriously. I think it is a reasonable proposal, and it would provide a demonstration of faith, hope and optimism, perhaps even some confidence in the farmers.
I have had some discussions earlier with the Parliamentary Secretary and there seems to be some consensus over there that this is a measure worthy of consideration. I think this motion would provide an excellent vehicle for looking at the whole area of farm input costs and the difficulties farmers are facing.
If it is agreeable, Mr. Speaker, I would be prepared to amend the motion to include the words:
That the subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for consideration.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) would second the motion, and if it meets with the approval of the House I would be prepared to submit that amendment for your consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend a few minutes supporting the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski). I think it would be of considerable assistance to the farmers of Canada. I would like to speak on behalf of the Saskatchewan agricultural community which finds the present energy costs much too high in terms of producing food. 1 will be very brief because the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mr. Waddell) wants to say a few words as well. We would also like to get this through the appropriate committee and subsequent stages.
The Hon. Member for Vegreville has outlined to the House a number of reasons why energy costs are becoming a real burden for farmers today. The price of wheat has not gone up in the last three or four years and farm input costs have skyrocketed. Interest rates have been very high for the farming community. Also the Crow rate has been abolished. The price of moving grain is going up by 500 per cent over the next nine years. Because of those things, there will have to be some support for the farmers.
I remember very well when, in the 1980 election campaign, as I am sure my friendly farmer friend from the Toronto airport riding recalls, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made a promise to the farmers. He said that if he was re-elected he would change evaluation day for capital gains on farms from December 31, 1971 to 1974 or 1976, which would take care of some of the inflationary problems. That was a campaign promise. We received some other capital gains changes on Wednesday, but the Government did not change evaluation day. I want to remind the Parliamentary Secretary of that since I know he is concerned about the farming population.

In terms of the precise motion before us today, I would like to put on the record figures showing where the energy dollar goes when people buy gasoline or diesel fuel for a tractor, car or truck. The figures I will use are October figures from a service station in Regina for leaded regular gasoline. The prices keep fluctuating and we had a different set of figures from the Hon. Member for Vegreville. These Figures are for a litre of gasoline which in October cost 40.2 cents in Regina, Saskatchewan. The federal share was 11.03 cents. That is made up of five or six items. The sales tax on this litre of gasoline was 2.89 cents. That is something we would like to see removed to help the farmers. There was an excise tax of 1.5 cents. The excise tax can be rebated to the farmers for farm fuel. This is useful to a number of farmers in my constituency, particularly smaller operators. More and more farmers are switching to diesel and as there is no excise tax on diesel the farm rebate on the excise tax is of no assistance.
The third thing the federal Government gets is the Canadian ownership charge which is charged on all gasoline. That works out to .72 cents a litre. The fourth thing is the wellhead royalty. That is 3.55 cents. The petroleum compensation
Agriculture
charge is 2.37 cents. The total moneys going to the federal Government on a 40 cent litre of gasoline was 11.03 cents.
In my province the provincial government also gets a share. The provincial government collects a royalty of 5.8 cents on each litre. We do not have any sales tax or other taxes above the 5.8 cents. The industry gets the lion's share. It gets 23.37 cents a litre in Saskatchewan. The industry's share is broken down in the following way. The ordinary retail dealer in Regina gets 3.27 cents. The refining, transportation and marketing of the crude oil amounts to another 10.26 cents. The transportation is .49 cents and the wellhead share is 9.35 cents.
That is the way a litre of gasoline is broken down. The federal Government takes about 11 cents, the province takes about 6 cents, and the industry takes about 23 cents. The total is around 40 cents. I think it would be useful if we were to accept the ideas expressed here by the Hon. Member for Vegreville and many other Members of the House to take off the federal share in order to stimulate the agricultural economy.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that the industry in the country basic to a healthy economy is the agricultural industry. If farming is going well, things will go very well in Montreal for my friend who sits across the way. If farming is going well, jobs will be created in the small business sector and the service industries. Farmers will buy tractors from Brantford. They will buy all kinds of combines and fertilizers. I think it is better for everyone. There is a tremendous spin-off effect from dollars spent in agriculture.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not be too long. This is a very important motion and a very welcome motion. Because I have been in the manufacturing and food business I can say that every dollar of the direct cost in production or manufacturing, by the time it goes through processing, handling, distribution, on to the retail shelf and into the cash register, it becomes $5. If the Government really means what it continues to say about improving our national productivity and about productivity being the answer for tomorrow and the return to a respectable place in the industrial world, then we must consider motions like this very seriously.
Therefore, I compliment the Member for Vegreville for bringing this motion forward and I thank the Members on the Government side for allowing the amendment to be moved.
I would also like to point out the troubles that we are experiencing on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts with our fishing industry and the cost problems we have there vis-a-vis other fishing nations. In light of the fact that we have to reduce costs and at the same time improve quality in packing and delivery of these food resources, I would like to move another amendment. It reads:
That on line 3 of the motion, after the word "farmers", we add the words "and fishermen".

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the proposal that we are hearing today. I believe it should go to committee for detailed study. I am glad that it was improved by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington).
I must say that the Member for Vegreville describes himself as an old horse trader and says that he likes to wheel and deal. We are seeing his talents here today. I suppose if he is an old horse trader he knows how to patch up an old nag and try to get it to look look good for the market. In this case, no matter how much he tries to patch it up, the Tory energy policy is so lame, so weak and so sick that not even a persuasive and charming old trader like him can make it look like a young filly. We have seen him make some energetic efforts today in an attempt to take us on on the Government side about some of our energy ideas. I categorize that as trying to take an old nag and turn it into a young filly.
Let us examine some of his remarkable efforts here. He reminded us of the prices that people are paying at the pump in his riding in Alberta and compared them with the prices that were being paid back in those dark but thankfully brief days when the Tories were in power. He forgot to mention that the Tories had a schedule of increases that were going to inch energy prices up after 1979.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: Never double.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: Things were not going to stay static. In fact, there were going to be big leaps. All of us in the House, as well as the Canadian people, remember that the Tory energy policy expressed in 1979 indicated that prices by now would be at least 85 per cent of the world level. They were then going to add 18 cents a gallon on top of that.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is not right, and you know it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF REMOVING FEDERAL SALES TAX ON FUELS USED FOR FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Furthermore, they were going to change the schedule so that the big increases came right at the beginning and the lower increases came at the end. We would have already paid those big increases by this time. Let us compare that with what the present Minister of Finance did with his national energy policy when he was Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He said that they should not go that high at all, and they do not go anywhere near that 85 per cent ceiling. Moreover, he said that those prices should include most of the charges that our hon. friend wanted to add on. Finally, the price increases were going to rise relatively smoothly. They were not going to take a big leap at the beginning and taper off at the end.
All of that resulted in people of my riding in Mississauga and, equally important, people in his riding of Vegreville paying less over the last four years for their energy than they ever would have paid under that Tory regime. Under that persuasive, charming but very expensive Tory regime, they would have paid far more if the Tories had followed through with those ideas in 1979 instead of acting in a compassionate way as we have done since 1980.
I would just like to point out this bete noire that Members on that side refer to all the time, namely, the Canadian ownership charge. What a terrible thing it is. First it is terrible, of course, because of the word "Canadian". Second, it is even more terrible because of the reference to ownership. Third, it costs people 4 cents a litre, by my calculation, opposed to the 18 cent surcharge that those on the other side were going to slap on.
I realize that it is not comfortable to defend a tax. I know that it never leaves the incumbent comfortable to be required to levy a tax, but I will say that I feel a lot better asking people to pay 4 cents so as ultimately to own something rather than paying 18 cents that will just go to the border and be shovelled out to a bunch of foreigners who happen to own the company at that time. I like keeping it inside Canada. That is why we have a Canadian ownership charge rather than an 18 cent a gallon foreign ownership charge.

If we come into the Finance Committee with this kind of idea, we clearly want to do things for food producers generally.
The first problem we are going to run into when we do this was typified by the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Capilano. It may not be a point of order, Mr. Speaker, but it is a fact which badly needs to be said. I appreciate hearing it from the Hon. Member. I am trying to illustrate the issue that on all tax exemptions we get everybody trying to cut in. Hon. Members all know this. They know the difficulty that arises out of a generous move which is later exploited by other people. We know, for example in my area, that there are lots of people who would love to call themselves farmers in order to get the benefits provided in the tax system for real farmers. The consequence is a complicated anti-avoidance section in the Income Tax Act. I am not sure that anybody will be able to come up with a better answer, although I look forward with interest to the results of the consultative committee announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his budget. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, if that committee sets up wide open tax avoidance opportunities, many non-farmers will try to take advantage. Equally, a lot of non-farmers will want to be called farmers if we show people how to cut the price of gas. We all know that. It is common sense. The committee will have to grapple with that problem. If the committee wants to have its report taken seriously, we will have to come up with a responsible answer to that question.
The second thing we will have to come up with, and it is alluded to by the capable Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), is how we are going to administer this. Do we go back to the purple gas system? If we are dealing with diesel fuel, we cannot do that.

Third, I want to point out that the costs are not as high as has been described here. My notes from the Finance Department tell me that if diesel fuel costs 35 cents a litre without any provincial road tax, then the federal sales tax is approximately 3 cents of that 35 cents. I understand that farmers can get 1.5 cents back on gasoline. There may be a system there that we can follow with diesel fuel as well. But if you can claim 1.5 cents back on a litre of gasoline, it shows the low impact this tax is having at that level. I would think the committee will have to ask: If we are going to require paper work both from the farmer and the private sector generally and from the Government, would it be worth it to set up this kind of routine? Those are serious questions that the committee is used to handling.
Finally, it is important to look at what has been done for farmers in the past week. We heard a misleading reference from the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) about the capital gains tax. It is clear in the farming community and in this House that farmers received a big bonus through the tax system in the recent Budget. We provided ways in that Budget for farmers to shelter up to $120,000 in capital gains by placing that in their RRSPs. They will not avoid the tax permanently, but clearly they can defer it for significant periods of time. They can spread out their income and claim it back at much lower rates of tax.
That is a far more flexible way to deal with the problem of capital gains than moving the valuation day would have been. This is a far superior kind of response. As one example, we do not get through our economy a variety of different valuation days. We get one valuation day continuing to be applied to everybody and a special measure that really helps farmers. Second, incorporated farmers will benefit from the new small business tax simplification measures. Third, farmers generally will benefit from the flexibility on the pension plans was proposed by the Minister of Finance.
Those are big improvements which members of the farming community from coast to coast recognize and are beginning to

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) made reference to horse traders. I know he is a literary man. Perhaps I could paraphrase Dr. Samuel Johnson by saying that a white horse and a Liberal are very similar: the first one is difficult to keep clean and the second one is difficult to keep honest. His speech on the Canadian ownership charge was something to behold. The Canadian ownership charge of four cents a gallon is a terrible charge, not because it is Canadian, ownership or a charge, but because it is there for no reason. It is there for the taking over of oil companies. The question I would have put to the Hon. Member if I had time is, which oil companies are they going to take over? This is not irrelevant, it is right on point. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said that we are not going to take over any more oil companies at the moment. The Government is collecting up to $800 million a year on a tax under false pretences. The Canadian ownership is a fraud, nothing more, nothing less.
If the Hon. Member wanted to attack the Conservative Party, he could have mentioned that the Conservative oil price was based on world price. That was the problem the Clark Government had. They were being whipsawed between the Premier of Ontario and the Premier of Alberta when trying to set an energy price. They opted for the world price. They moved toward it very rapidly and lost the election. I suspect the Hon. Member is here today because of that policy. He should have talked about the Liberal price being a blended price, which was not the world price but with all of these taxes it is becoming the world price.
Agriculture
I support this motion going to committee. I am an urban Member, although there are many retired farmers from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta in my riding. Also, our people feel instinctively that the Canadian farmer needs the best help we can give.
Last week I was at a nomination meeting in the Peace River district. I had conversations with our candidate, Elroy Diem-ert, and with Grant Notley, the Leader of our provincial Party, who is also the provincial Leader of the Opposition and some farmers there. I talked to the farmers. It became clear that they too were being whipsawed between the increase in the Crow rate, which the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) talked about, and some of the other increased costs such as this tax. Even a dumb urban Scot like me could get it through his thick head that this is a problem for the farmers. This is a good motion. It should go to committee.
This Government is prepared to advance all kinds of assistance to the oil companies in the form of PIP grants, $8 billion over the next four years is earmarked for PIP grants. The Budget gives further breaks to oil companies.

There are numerous grants for the major oil companies. There is also some assistance for large corporations and banks, but nothing for farmers.

This is a start. If we can tackle something that really affects the farmers who are being hurt by the increase in the Crow rate and because their energy costs are going up, and from what the Members from Alberta and Saskatchewan have been saying today, they are being hurt with the price they are getting for their produce, then this should go to committee.
I will conclude by saying that, when the Hon. Member said we should take the old nag and turn it into a young filly, I did not realize that he supported the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) running again for the Liberal leadership.
